21061-under-the-chilian-flag-a-tale-of-w:
Harry Collingwood set this sea tale in the war between Chile and Peru in the late 1870s, fought over a desert rich in nitrates. Two young Englishmen serve aboard the Pericles, a British steamer carrying nitrates, silver ore, and hides between Chilean ports and Liverpool. Their captain is so unpleasant that they decide to leave him.

Short of officers, the Chilean navy takes the two men on. What follows tracks their adventures and hardships in Chilean service during the war. Spanish ship names and local words colour the action. The result is a boys' naval story built on a real South American conflict.
21066-harry-escombe-a-tale-of-adventure-:
Harry Escombe works as a young draughtsman in a civil engineer's office. His firm wins a contract to survey and build a railway in Peru. Harry is picked to go, and success there could make his future. The man in charge of the project, though, is a deeply nasty character.

That chief sends Harry on a needlessly risky survey, and Harry falls from a cliff and is given up for dead. He survives in a coma, wakes among local people, and is taken for a returned Inca god. Worshipped in their city, he must somehow escape and find his way home to England.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KingMartinLuthe:
Henry P. Leifermann reported for United Press International from Memphis on an unusual demand. Humbert James Putt, a federal prisoner, insisted on testifying in the trial of James Earl Ray. A court had ruled Putt mentally incompetent. His claims touched both the King and Kennedy assassinations, and the wire described them as bizarre.

Big cases attract claimants from every margin, and Ray's trial drew its share. A prisoner demanding the stand with tales of two assassinations tested the court's patience and the wire's restraint. Leifermann's report preserves the episode as Memphis read it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MullenRobertRud:
Ron Rosenbaum wrote 'Wallowing in Watergate' about a document the Ervin Committee never released. The committee's staff had prepared a 46-page study of connections between Howard Hughes and Larry O'Brien. O'Brien chaired the Democratic National Committee, whose headquarters were burgled in the Watergate break-in. The study was deleted from the committee's output.

Rosenbaum asks why a finished staff study on Hughes and O'Brien was buried. Hughes money moved through the politics of both parties, and O'Brien had worked for Hughes. The article follows the deleted study as a story inside the larger scandal: work done, then suppressed, then reported on anyway. It is Watergate told through one missing document.
history-of-the-conquest-of-peru: William Hickling Prescott's 1847 masterpiece on Pizarro's conquest of the Inca Empire. Drawing on Spanish archives, the blind Boston historian turned a brutal conquest into epic narrative. Along with his Mexico, it remains the classic English account of the conquistadors.
lenin-development-capitalism-russia-1899:
Lenin wrote The Development of Capitalism in Russia in 1899, signing it with the name Vladimir Ilyin. The Russian original is the text held here. Narodnik writers had claimed that capitalism could not take root in peasant Russia. Lenin answers them with a mass of Russian statistics.

He shows markets, wage labor, and class splits already growing inside the village. That evidence formed the empirical base of Russian Marxism. The book grew from his Siberian exile studies and prison work. No public domain English translation exists, so the Russian stands alone. Readers with Russian meet the young Lenin as researcher. The data tables fill many pages.
nasa-tm-19660021939-application-of-a-dou:
S S Manson, J C Freche, and C R Ensign at Lewis Research Center applied a new fatigue rule in a paper for a crack meeting in Atlantic City in mid 1966. Parts under repeated load fail in two stages: a crack first forms, then it grows. Their double linear damage rule treats the two stages apart, each with its own straight-line damage count. Steel fatigue tests judge the rule.

Forecasting fatigue life decides when parts must be retired. A rule that fits both stages should forecast better than a single-line rule. Turbine and airframe parts live under exactly such repeated loads. The authors test their rule against real steel data, in a symposium devoted to crack growth, where rival methods met the same evidence.
nasa-tm-19680025225-the-solar-constant-a:
Goddard Space Flight Center teams measured the solar constant and solar spectrum from a research aircraft in August 1967, as this August 1968 report records. The NASA 711 Galileo experiment flew at about 38,000 feet. Flying high cut the air above the instruments, sharpening sunlight measurements. Matthew P. Thekaekara served as principal investigator for one interferometer instrument.

Dwight C. Kennard Jr. managed the project, with Raymond Kruger coordinating at Ames Research Center. Instruments included interferometers, a cone radiometer, and a filter radiometer. Charles H. Duncan and James J. Webb led thermophysics branch experiments. The report documents the flight program and its instrument teams. Precise solar output values anchor climate science and spacecraft thermal design.
nasa-tm-19690031067-seasonal-transitions:
J. S. Theon and W. S. Smith of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this September 1969 preprint, numbered X-621-69-393. They tracked seasonal transitions in the mesosphere's thermal structure at high latitudes. Acoustic grenade experiments, flown from Barrow, Alaska, timed sound echoes to profile middle air temperatures through the turning seasons.

Winter's disturbed features appeared high in the mesosphere in September, the pair report. Month by month they reached successively lower altitudes, until the full winter pattern stood by December. Then an early January warming at the stratopause began reversing the whole structure. That chain of events would in time restore the calm summertime case. Their watch ran from September 1968 through February 1969, catching both transitions.
nasa-tm-19720015325-spaceport-news-index:
The Kennedy Space Center Library issued this index on April 3, 1972, as report GP-969. Mrs Olive C Ankersen of the Documents Department compiled it. The index covers Spaceport News, the center's own newspaper. Its span runs from December 1962 through February 1972. Those years carried Kennedy from early Mercury work through the Apollo landings. The library aimed to capture that march of events for reference.

The index serves as a ready tool for finding names, places, and events. Together they make up the history of the Kennedy Space Center. Entries sit in alphabetical order by subject. Under each subject, the matching news items follow. Staff and historians could trace a person or program quickly. The foreword frames indexing as preserving history, not mere filing.
podcast-tuckercarlson-DPPla5e_fRU:
Tucker Carlson opens with the last scene of Orwell's Animal Farm. Pigs and men play cards together, hard to tell apart. He uses the image to judge the MAGA movement's fate.

The title warns of snakes in Washington warping the movement's meaning. Carlson argues leaders who once claimed rebellion now serve power. He asks what loyal voters should do next. The episode is a literary warning in plain form. It will speak to supporters who fear their win was stolen by the very swamp they fought. The warning lands harder for its calm tone.
podcast-tuckercarlson-s2T5ZNdsQrU:
Actor Charlie Sheen tells his craziest Hollywood stories to Tucker Carlson and explains why he rejects the official story of 9/11. Sheen, once TV's highest-paid star, lived a public meltdown before a quieter recovery. The bad boy holds court here in full, winning form.

Sheen recounts the wild years, the famous rants, and the cost of that fame. He lays out the questions that made him doubt the official account of the attacks. Carlson, a friend, draws out both the comedy and the candor. Amused and nostalgic viewers get a survivor of celebrity telling it his way.

the-treaty-of-the-european-union-maastri: The full text of the 1992 Maastricht Treaty, the agreement that created the European Union and set the path to the euro. Its articles lay out shared citizenship, a common foreign policy, and the rules for a single currency, reshaping a continent. Dry to read but historic in effect, it is the founding legal document of the modern EU.
